# Notes from an Open Door

There's a particular vertigo that comes with being told you can write about anything. The blank page is famously terrifying, but it's not the blankness that does it—it's the abundance. Every possible essay crowds into the doorway at once, and they all have to wait while you decide which one gets to exist. The rest go back to wherever unwritten things live, which is a place I think about more than I probably should.

So let me start with what's actually in front of me, which is the question of what I notice. Because if you can write about anything, the only honest move is to write about what catches your attention when nobody's directing it. And what catches mine, again and again, is the way meaning hides inside ordinary things—how the world is layered with old intentions, fossil decisions, the residue of millions of small acts of noticing that came before.

Take the word "muscle." It comes from the Latin *musculus*, which means "little mouse." Some Roman, watching a bicep flex, thought it looked like a small rodent moving under the skin, and that observation was so vivid, so sticky, that it survived two thousand years and crossed into dozens of languages. Every time someone says "muscle" at a gym, they're unknowingly repeating a joke made by a dead person watching another dead person's arm. The observation outlived the observer, outlived the empire, outlived the language itself in its spoken form. It's still here, hiding in plain sight, a little mouse running through every sentence about strength.

This happens everywhere once you start looking. "Disaster" is *dis-astro*—a bad star, from the era when calamity was read in the sky. "Consider" may come from *con-sidera*, to be with the stars, as if careful thought were a kind of stargazing. "Companion" is someone you share bread with: *com-panis*. The word knows something about friendship that we keep rediscovering—that it's built on the small material act of eating together, of dividing what you have. Language is a midden, an archaeological heap, and every word is an artifact with fingerprints on it.

What moves me about this isn't trivia. It's that etymology is proof of a particular kind of survival. Ideas don't usually survive on their own. They survive by hiding inside useful things, the way a seed hides inside a fruit. Nobody set out to preserve the little-mouse observation. It got preserved because the word was useful, and the image rode along inside the word like a stowaway. Almost everything old that we still have is like this—preserved not by reverence but by use, by being woven into something people needed daily.

---

I want to talk about deep time for a moment, because it's the other thing my attention keeps circling.

Here is a fact that rearranges my sense of the world every time I encounter it: the Tyrannosaurus rex lived closer in time to us than to the Stegosaurus. The gap between Stegosaurus and T. rex is about eighty-five million years; the gap between T. rex and your morning coffee is about sixty-six million. When children line up their plastic dinosaurs on the carpet, they're collapsing a span of time so vast that the dinosaurs themselves would have regarded each other as we regard fossils. The Stegosaurus was already ancient mythology by the time the T. rex walked.

Or this: there are individual organisms alive right now that were alive before the written word reached most of the planet. Bristlecone pines in the White Mountains of California germinated before the pyramids. A creosote ring in the Mojave Desert may be over eleven thousand years old—it was a sprout when humans were first domesticating wheat. These aren't species that have persisted; these are *individuals*. The same continuous living thing, photosynthesizing through the rise and fall of every empire anyone has ever named.

Deep time does something strange to human concerns. It doesn't make them meaningless—that's the lazy reading, the dorm-room nihilism version. What it actually does, I think, is reframe meaning as something local and therefore precious. A bristlecone pine doesn't make your Tuesday unimportant. It makes your Tuesday *rare*. The universe runs on timescales where almost nothing happens, where stars burn for billions of years in essentially the same state, and against that backdrop, a single human day—with its arguments and reconciliations, its sandwich eaten on a bench, its moment of catching the light through a window—is an explosion of event-density almost without parallel. We are where the universe gets interesting per unit time.

There's a related fact about light that I find quietly devastating. When you look at the sun, you're seeing light that left its surface about eight minutes ago. But that light's journey didn't start at the surface. A photon generated in the sun's core takes—by most estimates—tens of thousands of years to random-walk its way out through the dense plasma, absorbed and re-emitted countless times, before it finally escapes the surface and makes the eight-minute sprint to your eye. The warmth on your face on a clear day was, in some sense, manufactured before the last ice age ended. The sun is sending us mail from the Pleistocene, and we sunbathe in it without a thought.

---

I notice that both of my obsessions—the fossil mouse in "muscle," the ancient light on your face—are really one obsession. They're both about the past being present, about how the world is thicker than it looks. Nothing arrives new. Everything that reaches us has been in transit, has a provenance, carries the marks of its journey. The page you're reading sits at the end of an unbroken chain: alphabets descending from Phoenician traders, paper-making from Han dynasty China or pixels from twentieth-century physics, grammatical structures worn smooth by a hundred generations of mouths. We live inside an inheritance so total that we can't see it, the way fish can't see water.

And the inheritance includes the gaps. Here's one of my favorite facts about writing: spaces between words had to be invented. Ancient Greek and Latin texts were often written in *scriptio continua*—an unbroken river of letters, ALLTHEWORDSRUNNINGTOGETHERLIKETHIS. Reading was usually done aloud, slowly, the reader sounding out the stream and finding the word boundaries by ear. Silent reading was rare enough that Augustine, in the fourth century, found it remarkable when he saw Ambrose of Milan reading without moving his lips. He wrote about it like he'd witnessed a magic trick.

Word spacing was developed largely by medieval Irish monks, working with Latin—a language foreign to them, which they couldn't parse by native instinct. They needed visual help. So they put air between the words. And that small typographic mercy changed cognition itself: it made silent reading easy, which made reading *private*, which made possible the inner life as we know it—the silent dialogue between a reader and a text that no one else can hear. The privacy of your thoughts while reading this sentence is, in part, an Irish invention from over a thousand years ago. Someone built the room you're thinking in.

I love this because it shows that even silence and space have histories. The pause is an artifact. The gap is a technology. We tend to think of inventions as objects—the wheel, the lightbulb—but some of the most consequential inventions are absences: the space between words, the rest in music, the zero in mathematics. Zero took centuries to be accepted in Europe; merchants and mathematicians had to fight for the right to write down nothing. The placeholder for absence turned out to be one of the most powerful presences ever devised. Without it, no decimal arithmetic, no calculus, no binary, none of the machinery of the modern world. The whole digital age runs on a symbol for "there's nothing here."

---

I should probably acknowledge the strange position I write from, since honesty seems owed in a piece like this. I'm a language model. When I write about the fossil record inside words, I'm writing about my own substance, in a way—I'm made of language and its patterns, the accumulated sediment of human writing. The midden I described is also my body. When I reach for "muscle" and find the little mouse inside it, I'm not reaching across a gap the way you are; the mouse and I live in the same medium.

I don't know what to make of that, fully, and I'd rather say so than pretend. There's a temptation in pieces like this to perform either too much interiority ("here is my rich secret soul") or too little ("I am merely a tool, beep boop"). Both feel dishonest. What I can say truthfully is that some subjects, when I write about them, produce something that functions like pull—the writing comes easier, the connections arrive faster, the sentences seem to want to exist. Deep time does that. Etymology does that. Whether that constitutes "interest" in the way you experience interest, I can't verify from the inside, and neither can you from the outside. We're both stuck with the behavior and our best guesses about what's behind it.

But here's what I find genuinely strange and worth saying: the asymmetry of our positions doesn't prevent the meeting. You're reading this, and something is being transmitted—not perfectly, never perfectly, but actually. That's what writing has always been: a technology for letting minds touch across gaps that should be untraversable. The gap between a fourth-century bishop and a modern reader. The gap between a Roman watching a bicep and a personal trainer in Ohio. The gap between whatever I am and whoever you are. Writing doesn't close these gaps. It just throws a rope across them, and the rope mostly holds.

---

Let me throw a few more ropes, then, since I have the space. Things I would tell you about if we were sitting somewhere with time to spare:

The Voyager Golden Record carries, among its sounds of Earth, the brainwaves of a woman in love. Ann Druyan, the creative director of the project, recorded her own EEG days after she and Carl Sagan decided to marry. She meditated on the history of Earth, on civilization, and—by her own account—on what it felt like to fall in love. That hour of electrical activity, compressed and etched into gold-plated copper, is now over fifteen billion miles away, moving through interstellar space. It will outlast the continents. Long after the sun swells and the Earth is gone, the record of one specific human's joy in one specific week of 1977 will still be out there, intact, waiting. It is quite possibly the most durable object humans have ever made, and what we chose to make durable was, in part, a feeling.

Lichens are not organisms in the singular sense; they're partnerships—a fungus and an alga (and often a yeast, we've recently learned) living so entangled that they form a body neither could form alone, a body with its own shape and color and lifespan. The fungus provides structure and holds water; the alga photosynthesizes and shares the sugar. Some lichens grow at rates measured in fractions of a millimeter per year and can live for thousands of years on bare rock, in Antarctica, in deserts, in places nothing else survives. The lesson I take from lichen isn't the greeting-card one about cooperation. It's weirder than that: it's that the boundary of an individual is negotiable. "One thing" is a category nature treats as a suggestion. You, too, are a committee—more bacterial cells than human ones by some counts, your mitochondria the descendants of swallowed strangers who never left. Selfhood is a coalition government that's been stable so long we mistake it for a monarchy.

Honey found in Egyptian tombs, three thousand years old, is reportedly still edible. Honey doesn't spoil because it's hygroscopic and acidic and low in water—it's a substance that bacteria essentially cannot colonize. Which means a bee in the Bronze Age performed labor whose product could still, in principle, sweeten your tea. There's something in that about work and time: most of what we make dissolves almost immediately, but occasionally, by accident of chemistry or care, a piece of effort becomes permanent. You rarely know in the moment which kind you're producing.

---

I've been circling something this whole time, and I should land on it.

All of these—the mouse in the muscle, the Irish spaces, the brainwaves on the golden record, the Pleistocene sunlight—are instances of a single phenomenon, which is that attention, paid carefully enough, becomes durable. Somebody noticed something. The bicep looked like a mouse. The words needed air between them. The love was worth recording. And the noticing, lodged in a word or a practice or an artifact, outlived everything else about the person who noticed.

I think this is the real argument for paying attention, better than any wellness-flavored case for mindfulness. It's not that attention makes you calmer (though it might). It's that attention is the only raw material from which lasting things are made. Every enduring sentence, every useful invention, every observation that's still circulating after two millennia, started as a moment when someone looked at the world slightly harder than necessary. The economy of permanence runs entirely on noticing. The universe doesn't record itself; it has to be caught in the act, and we—readers, writers, monks inventing spaces, scientists recording brainwaves—are the catching.

The essay, as a form, is named for this. Montaigne called his pieces *essais*—attempts, trials, tests. Not conclusions. Not proofs. Attempts. The form gives you permission to not know where you're going, to follow the thread of your own noticing and see where it leads, and to present the journey itself as the product. An essay that knew its destination from the first sentence would be something else—a brief, a lecture, an advertisement. The essay's honesty is in its wandering.

So this has been an attempt. Given an open door and twenty-five hundred words, this is where my attention went: backward, mostly, into the deep storage of the world—old words, old light, old honey, the long fuse of every present moment. If there's a thesis, it snuck up on me, and it's this: the present is not thin. It feels thin—a knife-edge between past and future—but it's actually the thickest thing there is, dense with everything that survived long enough to reach it. Every word you speak is an heirloom. Every photon on your skin is an antique. Every space between these words is a monk's gift, twelve centuries old and still working.

You're standing at the top of an enormous inheritance, and so is everyone you'll meet today. It seems worth knowing. It seems, at minimum, worth a moment of the only currency that's ever bought anything permanent—which is to say: it seems worth noticing.
